questions.title: Closure captures outer variable
questions.explanation:
Output: 10
inner() closes over x in outer's scope. Even after outer() returns, inner retains a reference to x = 10 through its closure. This is the core of how closures work — inner keeps the scope alive.

questions.title: Returned closure retains value
questions.explanation:
Output: Hello, Alice
makeGreeter returns a function that closes over name. Even after makeGreeter has returned, the inner function still holds a reference to name = "Alice" in its closure scope.

questions.title: Independent closure instances
questions.explanation:
Output: 1
a and b are completely independent closures — each call to counter() creates a new execution context with its own n. a's calls increment a's n (now 2). b() increments b's own n from 0 to 1.

questions.title: Classic var loop trap
questions.explanation:
Output: 3 3 3
var is function-scoped — all three closures share the exact same i variable. By the time setTimeout callbacks run (after the loop), i has already been incremented to 3. All three closures read 3.

questions.title: let loop — does it change?
questions.explanation:
Output: 0 1 2
let is block-scoped. Each loop iteration creates a brand new binding of i — a separate variable in its own block scope. Each closure captures its own copy: 0, 1, 2.

questions.title: Closure mutation — shared reference
questions.explanation:
Output: 8
Both add and get close over the same sum variable. add(5) mutates sum → 5, add(3) mutates it → 8. get() reads the latest value: 8. This demonstrates how closures can share mutable state.

questions.title: Closure inside object method
questions.explanation:
Output: Hi from Bob
greet() creates msg = "Hi from Bob" and returns a function that closes over msg. When fn() is called later, it still has access to msg through its closure. name is also in scope via the outer closure from person().

questions.title: IIFE captures loop variable
questions.explanation:
Output: 0 1 2
The IIFE (function(j){...})(i) is called immediately on each iteration, passing i by value into j. Each IIFE creates its own scope with its own j (0, 1, 2). The returned function closes over j — not i — so each captures a distinct value.
questions.concept: IIFE to fix var loop trap

questions.title: Closure over mutated outer variable
questions.explanation:
Output: 2
The closure captures a reference to x, not a snapshot of its value. When x is reassigned to 2 after fn is created, the closure sees the updated value. Closures close over the variable binding, not the value at creation time.

questions.title: Stale closure in setTimeout
questions.explanation:
Output: 3
count is a global variable. inc() is called three times synchronously before the setTimeout fires. The closure inside setTimeout closes over count in the global scope — but count has already been mutated to 3 by then. Output: 3.

questions.title: Function factory — which value?
questions.explanation:
Output: 24
triple(4) calls the closure where x=3, y=4 → returns 12. double(12) calls the closure where x=2, y=12 → returns 24. Each closure independently captures its own x.

questions.title: Returning closure that modifies closure
questions.explanation:
Output: 2
All three methods close over the same val. inc() × 3 → val = 3. dec() × 1 → val = 2. log() prints 2. This is the classic Module Pattern — shared private state via closure.

questions.title: Shadowed variable in nested closure
questions.explanation:
Output: "inner" "outer" "global"
Each function has its own x that shadows the outer x. inner() logs its own local x = "inner". After inner() returns, outer() logs its own x = "outer". The global console.log sees the global x = "global". Variable shadowing — not mutation.

questions.title: Closure + immediately returned function
questions.explanation:
Output: 15 20 25
The IIFE runs once, setting x = 10 and returning a closure. fn is that closure. Each call increments x by 5: 10+5=15, 15+5=20, 20+5=25. x persists across calls because it lives in the IIFE's scope, captured by the closure.

questions.title: Tricky: closure in array methods
questions.explanation:
Output: 27
var i is shared across all closures. After the loop, i = 3. arr[0]() = 3*3 = 9, arr[1]() = 9, arr[2]() = 9. Total = 27. Classic trap — all functions see the final i = 3, not their loop-time value.

questions.title: Closure with conditional reassignment
questions.explanation:
Output: true
check closes over the variable flag (a reference). flag is reassigned to false, then to true. When test()() is called, flag = true at that point. The closure always sees the current value of the variable, not any snapshot.

questions.title: Nested closure — which x wins?
questions.explanation:
Output: 2
c() looks up x in the scope chain: first checks c's own scope (no x), then b's scope (x = 2) — found. Stops there. a's x = 1 is never reached. This is lexical scoping: the nearest enclosing scope wins.

questions.title: Closure inside a callback
questions.explanation:
Output: 40
forEach uses a callback, and each callback's item parameter is a new binding for each iteration (like let). fns[1] closes over item = 20. fns[1]() returns 20 * 2 = 40. Note: forEach callback parameters are always per-iteration, regardless of var/let.
